confusionCorner.body: The Zero-Product Property only works when the product equals [[imp:zero]]. If the product equals, say, 5, you can't conclude anything about the factors. That's why we always move all terms to one side to make it equal 0 before factoring.
confusionCorner.title: Why Must One Side Be Zero?

teacherCues: Write 'ab = 0' on the board. Ask: 'If the product of two numbers is zero, what must be true?'
Show 2x(x-4)=0 and say: 'Set each factor equal to zero and solve — that's the whole secret.'
blocks.title: Zero-Product Property

examples.title: Example A — Basic Equation
steps: The equation is already in factored form with 0 on the right side.
Set each factor equal to zero: $x-3=0$ or $x-9=0$.
Solve: $x=3$ or $x=9$. The roots are $3$ and $9$.

The roots are 9 and 1; which is larger?

discoveryHook.scenario: If you multiply two numbers and get zero, at least one of them must be zero. This simple idea — the Zero-Product Property — is one of the most powerful tools in algebra. Once a polynomial equation is written as a product of factors equal to zero, the solutions practically jump out!

notes: Works for any number of factors: $abc = 0$ means $a=0$, $b=0$, or $c=0$.
Always rewrite the equation so one side equals 0 before factoring.
formulaCard.title: Zero-Product Property

explanation: A polynomial is in [[kw:factored form]] when it is written as a product of factors. Example: $x(x+2)$ is factored; $x^2+2x$ is standard form.
The [[kw:Zero-Product Property]] states: If $a$ and $b$ are real numbers and $ab = 0$, then $a = 0$ or $b = 0$.
To solve an equation like $(x-3)(x-9)=0$, set each factor equal to zero: $x-3=0$ or $x-9=0$.
The solutions are also called [[kw:roots]] of the equation.
[[imp:One side must be 0, and the other side must be a product.]] This property only works for zero!

questions.prompt: When an equation like $(x-3)^2=0$ gives the same solution twice, the root is called a ___ root.
Solve $ (2a-6)(3a+15) = 0 $. What is the smallest root?

hints: Count the factors that are different.
Set each factor to zero and see if any are the same.

blocks.title: Repeated Roots and Multiple Factors

discoveryHook.scenario: Sometimes an equation like (x-1)² = 0 gives the same answer twice. We say it has a repeated root. The graph touches the x-axis but doesn't cross — the root has multiplicity 2. And when three factors multiply to zero, you get three roots!

formulaCard.title: Repeated Roots
notes: A root repeated twice is a double root.
The graph touches the x-axis at a repeated root but does not cross.

explanation: When two or more roots of an equation are the same number, the equation has [[kw:repeated roots]].
Example: $(x-1)^2 = 0$ expands to $(x-1)(x-1)=0$, giving $x=1$ twice — a repeated root.
The Zero-Product Property extends to any number of factors. For $(x+1)(x-3)(x-2)=0$, you set each factor to zero: $x=-1$, $x=3$, $x=2$.
If a factor has a coefficient, like $(2x+7)$, solve as usual: $2x+7=0$ → $x=-7/2$.

teacherCues: Write (x-1)² = 0. Ask: 'How many factors do you see? How many solutions will we get?'
Explain that (x-1)² means (x-1)(x-1), so both factors give the same root — it's a repeated root.

confusionCorner.body: In $(2x+7)=0$, you must solve $2x+7=0$, not just $x+7=0$. The coefficient [[imp:stays attached]] to the variable until you isolate it.
confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget the Coefficient

teacherCues: Write 4x⁴ + 24x³ on the board. Ask: What's the largest number that divides 4 and 24? What's the highest power of x common to both terms?

confusionCorner.body: When factoring $4x^3(x+6)$, the parentheses contain a binomial. If you factor out the entire term, the remaining factor for that term is 1. Example: $x + x^2 = x(1 + x)$, not $x(x)$.
confusionCorner.title: Don't Forget the Hidden 1!

formulaCard.title: Factoring Out the GCF
notes: Always factor out the GCF completely — don't leave common factors behind.
After factoring, the remaining polynomial should have no common factors other than 1.

explanation: To factor a polynomial, look for the [[kw:greatest common factor (GCF)]] of its terms — a monomial that divides every term evenly.
The GCF includes the largest number that divides all coefficients, and the smallest exponent of each variable common to all terms.
Example: $4x^4 + 24x^3$: GCF of coefficients 4 and 24 is 4; GCF of $x^4$ and $x^3$ is $x^3$. So GCF = $4x^3$.
Factor it out: $4x^3(x + 6)$. Check by distributing to ensure you get the original.
After factoring, you can set each factor to zero to solve the equation.

Find GCF of variables: smallest exponent of $x$ is 3, so $x^3$.

discoveryHook.scenario: Before you can use the Zero-Product Property, the equation must be in factored form. But many polynomials are given in standard form! The first step to factoring is pulling out the Greatest Common Factor (GCF) — the monomial that divides each term.

blocks.title: Solving Equations by Factoring

confusionCorner.title: Don't Divide by the Variable!
confusionCorner.body: In $3n^2 = 9n$, if you divide both sides by $n$, you get $3n = 9$ and miss the solution $n=0$. Always bring all terms to one side and [[imp:factor, don't divide]], to preserve all roots.

questions.feedbackIfWrong: One side must be zero to use the Zero-Product Property.
questions.prompt: Before factoring, you must rewrite the equation so that one side equals ___.
hints: The Zero-Product Property only works when the product equals this number.

questions.prompt: Solve $ 4p^2 - p = 0 $. What is the nonzero root?
In the equation $ 3s^2 - 9s = 0 $, what is the root that is a positive integer?

notes: One root is always $x=0$ when there is no constant term.
Never divide both sides by $x$ — you'll lose the root $x=0$.
formulaCard.title: Solving by Factoring (GCF Method)

explanation: To solve a polynomial equation using the Zero-Product Property, you may first need to [[imp:factor]] the polynomial.
Step 1: Move all terms to one side so the equation equals 0.
Step 2: Factor out the GCF. Step 3: Set each factor equal to 0 and solve.
Always check that you didn't divide by a variable when solving — you might lose a root of 0!

discoveryHook.scenario: Many polynomial equations don't start with zero on one side. They look like $6n^2 = 15n$. Before factoring, we must rewrite them as something = 0. Then we factor out the GCF, apply the Zero-Product Property, and the solutions appear!

examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why can't we just divide both sides by $n$? What root would we lose, and why is that a problem?
examples.title: Example B — Move Terms First

teacherCues: Write 2x² + 8x = 0. Factor out 2x → 2x(x+4)=0. Now use Zero-Product Property.
For 6n² = 15n, move all terms to one side first: 6n² - 15n = 0. Then factor and solve.

hints: The answer is the larger root.

formulaCard.title: Width from a Factored Quadratic
notes: The roots $r_1$ and $r_2$ are the x-intercepts.
The constant factor $k$ does not affect the roots.

explanation: Real-world objects like arches, tunnels, and bridges can be modeled by quadratic equations in factored form.
The width at ground level is the distance between the points where the graph crosses the x-axis (where $y=0$).
Step 1: Set $y=0$ and solve for $x$. Step 2: The solutions are the x-intercepts. Step 3: The width is the absolute difference between the two x-values.

confusionCorner.body: Width is always positive. After finding the two x-intercepts, subtract them and take the absolute value. If you get a negative width, you subtracted in the wrong order.
